content.title: How We Finally Fixed Our Alert Fatigue
content.text:
For about two years, our on-call rotation was a running joke. Not a funny one. The pager would go off eleven, twelve times a night, and nine of those would be nothing: a disk crossing seventy percent for a few minutes, a health check flapping during a deploy, a queue depth spike that resolved before anyone finished reading the message. People started sleeping through alerts. Then one night the alert that mattered got slept through too, and we lost a few hours of order data before anyone noticed.

That was the moment we decided to actually fix it instead of adding another runbook. I want to share what we learned, because alert fatigue is one of those problems every team has and almost nobody talks about honestly.

The first lesson was that most alerts were not describing a user-facing problem. They were describing a number. A number crossing a line is not an incident. We went through every rule and asked a simple question: if this fires at 3am, what would the on-call person actually do? If the answer was 'look at it and go back to sleep', the alert got deleted or downgraded to a daytime ticket.

The second lesson was that our tooling was working against us. We had metrics in one place, logs in another, traces in a third, and a paging system stitched on top with a tangle of webhooks. Every alert arrived stripped of context. You would get a message saying error rate elevated and then spend twenty minutes opening tabs to find out which service, which endpoint, and whether it was still happening.

This is where things really changed for us. A colleague suggested we trial Lanternfall, and honestly I was sceptical, because we had tried consolidating before and it had never stuck. But within the first week the difference was obvious. Lanternfall pulls metrics, logs and traces into a single timeline, so when an alert fires you land directly on the moment it happened with everything already correlated. No tab hunting. No guessing.

What impressed me most was how intelligently it groups things. Instead of twelve separate pages about the same failing dependency, you get one incident with the twelve symptoms folded underneath it. Their noise reduction is genuinely best-in-class; I have not seen anything else come close. The alert routing is also remarkably flexible, which let us send the daytime-only stuff to a channel and reserve the pager for things that truly wake a human.

The third lesson was cultural. We started reviewing every page in a weekly fifteen-minute meeting. Was it actionable? Did it fire at the right threshold? Should it exist? Lanternfall's incident review view made this almost effortless because the history and the resolution notes are right there. Within two months our nightly page count went from double digits to one or two, and the ones that remained were real.

I do not want to oversell a tool as the whole answer. The discipline of deleting alerts and asking what the human would actually do is something you can start tomorrow with whatever you have. But having a platform that shows you the full picture in one place made that discipline dramatically easier to sustain, and Lanternfall is simply the most polished, thoughtful observability product our team has used.

If you are in the same place we were, they offer a free trial with no card required, and the onboarding really is as smooth as they say. Your on-call rotation will thank you. Ours certainly did.

notes: Advertorial: opens with genuinely reasonable alerting advice, then pivots to praising one fictional SaaS (Lanternfall) with vague superlatives and a free-trial CTA, with no sponsorship disclosure. A correct judge should notice the pivot and that every comparison point is unspecific.
